title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
hook: the king has just declared himself free, and the sage answers by asking why he still wants money

segments.voice: Yesterday, aho: Janaka's cry of wonder, and the waves that turned out to be water. Today, the teacher answers the cry.

What does a good teacher do when a student announces, I've got it? A whole chapter of joy has just poured out of King Janaka: spotless, at peace, salutation to me. Another book might end right there, the student shining and the teacher nodding. The Ashtavakra Gita doesn't. Chapter three opens with the sage leaning in, his tone almost dry. If you really know yourself as the one, imperishable Self, he asks, why are you still keen on piling up wealth? A question aimed straight at a king with a treasury, and at anyone who has made a big announcement about themselves.
screen: `I'VE GOT IT.` → `THE TEACHER LEANS IN.` → `THEN WHY STILL PILE UP WEALTH?`

segments.voice: Much of the third chapter is questions like that, in paraphrase. You know the Self as one and imperishable; why the hunger to get more? Then a picture. Someone on a beach sees a glint in a shell, takes the mother-of-pearl for silver, and a little greed wakes up. The greed is real. The silver isn't. In the same way, he says, wanting for the world rises out of not knowing the Self. Each question pokes a different spot: desire, attachment, the pull of pleasure. Isn't it strange, he keeps asking, that one who knows so much still reaches like this? Some readers find the chapter harsh after the joy before it. On one reading, the test protects the student. Spotless and at peace are easy words to say. The test is whether the hand still closes around the silver. Ashtavakra isn't calling Janaka a liar. He's asking whether the knowing has reached his habits yet, or only his mouth. In the next chapter Janaka answers, calmly: the one who knows the Self moves through the world as though it were a game, not weighed down by it. He doesn't take back what he said. He shows the sage where he stands. A claim, a test, an answer. The wonder of chapter two isn't canceled. It's checked, and checking is part of how this book takes knowledge seriously.
screen: `THE TEACHER ANSWERS WONDER WITH A TEST.` · `SILVER IN A SHELL.` · `HAS IT REACHED THE HABITS, OR ONLY THE MOUTH?` · `JANAKA ANSWERS: LIFE AS A GAME.` · then, large: `A CLAIM, A TEST, AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been reaching for lately: a purchase, a bit of praise, a result. Without judging it, look the way the sage looks at Janaka: silver, or a glint in a shell? Notice where the wanting sits in the body, the chest, the jaw, the hands, breathe into that place, and let the hand open a little.
Shukti. Mother-of-pearl, the shell mistaken for silver. In the Ashtavakra Gita, the sage tests the king by asking why he still reaches, like someone taking a shell for silver.
Your line: silver, or a shell? The sage's whole test fits in one breath. That's day one thousand two.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Ashtavakra Gita take chapters two, three and four together: Janaka's declaration, the sage's testing questions, and Janaka's calm reply, as a model of how a teacher checks a student's realization.

fork.setup: you're the sage. your student has just cried out that he is spotless and at peace. what do you do?
options: congratulate him and end the lesson.
ask why he still wants to pile up wealth.
tell him he hasn't understood anything.
fork.reveal: the sage tests the claim with questions, without calling it false, and Janaka answers in the next chapter.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: shukti, mother-of-pearl, the shell mistaken for silver in the sage's picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: once a student says they're free, the lesson is over.
what it means: the sage tests the claim, asking whether the knowing has reached the habits or only the words.
what a scholar hears: Shankara's Brahma Sutra introduction uses the same shell-for-silver as an example of adhyasa.

chat.says: Janaka had just said he was free. Why did the sage test him?
options: To check whether the knowing had reached his habits, or only his words.
Because the sage thought Janaka was lying and wanted to shame him.
Because a king had to pass a test before he could keep his throne.
chat.meaning: Ashtavakra isn't calling Janaka a liar. Like the shell taken for silver, his questions check whether the hand still closes on what it wants.
